title: Unsung women

segments.voice: Yesterday: failures too, the tradition naming its own worst days, and Adam and his wife saying we have wronged ourselves. Your line was honesty is faith.

Mecca, a room within reach of the sanctuary. A woman sits with a book open in front of her. Across from her, men with pens and paper, scholars who traveled to be here. She reads Bukhari's collection of hadith aloud, line by line, and they copy it down, checking every word against what they hear, so that later they can say: I heard it from her. Her name is Karima al-Marwaziyya, and it went into the chain by which that book was passed on. Women were in this history the whole way through, often doing the work while someone else got the chapter. Today: unsung women.
screen: `A WOMAN READS; SCHOLARS WRITE.` → `I HEARD IT FROM HER.` → `THE WORK, WITHOUT THE CHAPTER.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an sets the frame. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! I suffer not the work of any worker, male or female, to be lost." The chronicles might drop a name; the verse says the work isn't dropped. So pick some back up, four kinds, all names this path has met. First, a founder. In Fez, tradition says a woman named Fatima al-Fihri used her inheritance to found the mosque that became al-Qarawiyyin, a place of study. Second, a teacher: Karima, in that room in Mecca, whose reading of Bukhari's collection men traveled to hear. Third, a poet. In Sokoto, Nana Asma'u wrote poems in several languages to teach the faith, and trained women teachers who carried those lessons to women in villages far from her. Fourth, a patron. Zubayda, wife of the caliph Harun al-Rashid, whose name tradition gives to the wells and stations of the pilgrim road from Iraq to Mecca, and other women after her who paid for schools, fountains and mosques with their own wealth, their names cut into stone over doors that passersby rarely stop to read. Founders, teachers, poets, patrons. The history needed them and often forgot to say so. And the lesson isn't only about the past: in any mosque, school or family today, someone is doing work that nobody writes down.
screen: `NO WORKER'S WORK IS LOST, MALE OR FEMALE.` · `A FOUNDER: FATIMA AL-FIHRI IN FEZ.` · `A TEACHER AND A POET: KARIMA, NANA ASMA'U.` · `A PATRON: ZUBAYDA'S WELLS.`

segments.voice: Say today's names slowly, one per breath: Zubayda, Fatima, Karima, Asma'u. Then think of the woman in your own story whose work made something possible and never got the credit, a mother, a teacher, an aunt who taught the prayers, a colleague who did the unseen part, and say her name too, quietly, if you know it.
Unsung women. The founders, teachers, poets and patrons whose work built Muslim history, often without the credit. Today's word.
Your line: they were there. The work wasn't lost, even when the name was. Day one thousand fifty-three, done.

howItsDone: Muslim communities remember women such as Khadijah, Aisha and Fatimah from the Prophet's household, and local histories honor women who founded mosques, schools and charitable endowments.

Zubayda, Fatima al-Fihri, Karima al-Marwaziyya and Nana Asma'u were each taught earlier this year (days 914/1045, 916/919, 1032, 975); this day gathers them as a reflection and repeats only claims made there. Fatima's founding is framed as 'tradition says'.
'Nana Asma'u wrote poems in several languages' follows day 975 (Arabic, Fulfulde, Hausa).
'Other women after her who paid for schools, fountains and mosques' is a general statement about endowments (waqf), with no names or counts.
